# **1\. Executive Summary**

Tolly is an AI-powered audio companion for children aged 4 to 12\. It is a screen-free toy that listens, talks, and learns alongside a child.

Tolly is built on conversational AI. It responds to a child's mood. It supports learning. It shares key behavioural insights with parents.

We are at the MVP stage. A working product exists. Early users have responded positively. We are now raising a Seed Round to build our full platform.

# **2\. The Problem**

Parents want to support their child’s development. But they cannot always be present. This creates a gap.

**Working parents face a particular challenge.** Long working hours mean that meaningful overlap with their children is often limited to evenings and weekends. During the rest of the day, children are left without the active presence, guidance, and enrichment that parents would otherwise provide. This time is largely lost.

The tools available today do not fill that gap well:

* Screens overstimulate young children.

* Educational apps require adult supervision to be effective.

* Toys do not adapt to a child's emotional state or learning needs.

* Parents have limited visibility into how their child is feeling or behaving when they are not around.

The result: children miss out on enrichment time, and parents feel less in control of their child's development during the hours they are apart.

# **3\. The Solution — Tolly**

Tolly is a screen-free AI companion. It sits with a child and talks with them — like a toy that truly listens.

Tolly is different because it:

* Adapts its responses to the child's mood in real time.

* Supports learning through natural conversation, not structured lessons.

* Extends the parent's values and parenting style, even when the parent is not in the room.

* Shares a regular summary with parents, highlighting any negative emotions or behavioural patterns.

* Allows parents to guide Tolly on how to respond to specific situations.

* Encourages children to express their emotions and process their experiences in a safe, supportive space.

* Allows parents to delegate rule enforcement to Tolly — freeing them to enjoy their parenting time rather than spending it on discipline.

Tolly has no screen. It is audio only. This makes it safe, simple, and non-addictive for young children.

# **5\. Market Opportunity**

The global market for children's educational technology is large and growing. Parents are actively seeking tools that are screen-free, personalised, and safe.

Tolly sits at the intersection of three growing markets:

* EdTech — digital tools for children's learning.

* Smart Toys — connected, AI-enabled physical products for children.

* Parental Technology — tools that give parents insight and control over their child's development.

Our primary target is parents of children aged 4 to 12 in English-speaking markets. This is a high-spending demographic that prioritises both education and wellbeing.

Tolly's screen-free, audio-first design gives it a clear advantage. There is no direct competitor that combines mood-adaptive AI, learning support, and parental oversight in a single product.

# **13\. Why Tolly Is Difficult to Replicate**

Tolly is built with a set of technical and operational choices that protect its position. These are not features that can be quickly copied. They are foundational decisions made at the design stage.

| Differentiator | What It Means in Practice |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Safety Guardrails** | Multi-layer content safety is built into the product architecture. Every response is filtered before it reaches the child. Parents can set additional restrictions at any time. |
| **Offline Classifiers** | Key safety and mood-detection models run locally on the device. This means Tolly continues to work reliably even without an internet connection, protecting both uptime and user privacy. |
| **Cost-Controlled AI Architecture** | Tolly’s AI is designed to avoid token cost inflation as usage grows. A hybrid on-device and cloud model keeps variable costs low and margins healthy at scale. |
| **Built-In Expert Support** | Parents have access to a team of experts — in child development, psychology, education, and parenting — who can respond to specific concerns. This human layer adds trust and depth that a pure-AI product cannot replicate. |
| **Shareable Parent Summaries** | Parents can share Tolly’s child summaries directly with third-party professionals they already work with — such as parenting coaches, therapists, or educators — creating a connected support network around the child. |

# **Glossary of Terms**

The following terms are used in this document. They are explained here for ease of reference.

| Term | Definition |
| :---- | :---- |
| **MVP (Minimum Viable Product)** | An early version of the product with just enough features to test the concept with real users. It is used to gather feedback before building the full product. |
| **Seed Round** | The first official round of investment a business raises. It is used to move from an early idea or prototype to a working business. |
| **SaaS (Software as a Service)** | A way of selling software where the customer pays a regular subscription fee (monthly or yearly) rather than buying it once. |
| **EdTech** | Short for Educational Technology. It refers to products and services that use technology to support learning and education. |
| **D2C (Direct-to-Consumer)** | A sales model where a company sells its product directly to customers, without using a shop or third-party retailer as a middleman. |
| **B2B (Business-to-Business)** | Selling products or services to other businesses (e.g. schools or nurseries) rather than directly to individual consumers. |
| **Go-To-Market (GTM)** | The plan a business uses to launch a product and reach its target customers. |
| **Conversational AI** | Artificial intelligence technology that can hold a natural conversation with a person — listening to what they say and responding in a human-like way. |
| **COPPA** | Children's Online Privacy Protection Act. A US law that restricts the collection of personal data from children under 13\. |
| **GDPR-K** | An extension of European data protection law (GDPR) that applies specifically to children's data. |
| **Traction** | Evidence that a product is gaining real interest or use in the market. It can include users, revenue, or positive feedback. |
| **Recurring Revenue** | Income that a business receives on a regular basis (e.g. monthly subscriptions). It is predictable and valuable to investors. |
| **Early Adopters** | The first customers to try a new product. Their feedback shapes how the product develops. |
| **LTV (Lifetime Value)** | The total amount of money a business expects to earn from a single customer over the entire time they use the product. |
| **CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost)** | The cost of gaining one new customer, including marketing and sales expenses. |
| **Valuation** | The estimated total worth of a company, agreed between the founders and investors at the time of investment. |

# **Parents of 4–8-year-olds in the U.S. feel “out of control”**

Parents in the United States with children aged 4–8 often experience a persistent sense of **losing control over time, routines, and outcomes**. This isn’t due to a single factor—but a collision of developmental demands, shifting parenting roles, and systemic constraints.

A useful way to understand this is through **four reinforcing dimensions**:

---

# **1\. Children’s needs are rapidly expanding and diversifying**

Between ages 4–8, children undergo **simultaneous growth across multiple domains**, each demanding active parental involvement:

### **🧠 Emotional & behavioral**

* Children are still developing **self-regulation**, leading to tantrums, defiance, and impulsivity  
* According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, this is a critical period for emotional skill-building

> “Early childhood is when foundational self-regulation skills are built—and when problems first emerge.”

* \~**10–15% of children** show notable behavioral challenges at this stage

---

### **🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Social development**

* Learning friendships, cooperation, and conflict resolution  
* Early peer rejection is linked to later anxiety (research summarized by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)

---

### **📚 Academic / school readiness**

* Transition to structured learning environments  
* Major milestone: **learning to read by Grade 3**  
* National Assessment of Educational Progress data shows:  
  * Only \~**1 in 3 U.S. 4th graders** are proficient in reading

> “Achievement gaps that appear in early elementary school tend to persist.” — National Institute for Early Education Research

---

### **🎯 Extracurricular & foundational skill-building**

* Parents feel pressure to build:  
  * Cognitive skills (reading, math)  
  * Physical skills (sports)  
  * Creative skills (music, art)

👉 Result: **Children’s needs are no longer singular—they are parallel and compounding**

---

# **2\. The parenting role is becoming more complex and psychologically demanding**

As children grow, parenting shifts from **managing behavior → shaping minds**

### **Key transitions**

#### **🧠 Emotional coaching replaces simple discipline**

* Parents must teach:  
  * Emotional regulation  
  * Empathy  
  * Problem-solving

#### **📏 Routine enforcement becomes critical**

* Sleep, school prep, homework, meals all require consistency  
* Inconsistent routines are linked to behavior issues (AAP-backed research)

---

#### **📱 Digital gatekeeping becomes a daily battle**

* Common Sense Media:  
  * Kids 5–8 spend \~**3+ hours/day on screens**

> “Parents are now media managers, not just caregivers.”

---

#### **🧑‍🏫 Increased involvement in learning**

* Harvard Graduate School of Education research shows:  
  * Parental involvement improves outcomes—but **raises stress levels significantly**

---

👉 Result: Parenting becomes **mentally taxing, constant, and ambiguous**  
There are no clear “rules,” only continuous judgment calls

---

# **3\. The environment remains structurally unaccommodating**

While parenting demands increase, **external systems have not adapted accordingly**

---

### **⏰ Work pressures remain high**

* Pew Research Center:  
  * \~**60% of parents feel rushed** most of the time  
* American Time Use Survey:  
  * Parenting time has increased significantly over decades, despite similar work hours

---

### **💸 Childcare and support are expensive and fragmented**

* Child Care Aware of America:  
  * Costs can reach **$10,000–$20,000/year per child**  
* U.S. Census Bureau:  
  * Families rely on **patchwork solutions** (aftercare \+ relatives \+ paid help)

---

### **🚗 Rigid logistics dominate daily life**

* Fixed school hours vs work schedules  
* Extracurriculars require:  
  * Pickup/drop  
  * Strict time slots  
  * Parental coordination

---

### **🏠 Household responsibilities remain unchanged**

* Meals, cleaning, errands still need to be managed  
* No structural reduction despite increased parenting demands

---

👉 Result: Parents operate in a system where **everything is rigid except their time**

---

# **4\. Parents have little time or capacity to regain control**

With pressure from all sides, parents are left with **minimal recovery space**

---

### **😴 Sleep deprivation & burnout**

* The American Psychological Association reports:  
  * Parents have **higher stress levels than non-parents**  
* The U.S. Surgeon General (2024 advisory):

> “Parental stress is a significant public health issue.”

---

### **🧘 No time for self-regulation or support**

* Parents lack time to:  
  * Seek coaching or guidance  
  * Reflect on parenting strategies  
  * Invest in their own mental health

---

### **🔁 Trapped in “logistics \+ conflict management”**

* Days are spent:  
  * Coordinating schedules  
  * Managing child resistance (bedtime, homework, screens)  
  * Reacting instead of planning

---

### **🧠 Cognitive overload**

* Constant decisions across:  
  * School  
  * Health  
  * Discipline  
  * Activities

👉 Result: Parents are **operationally busy but strategically stuck**

Impact on kids:

Children don’t just attach to a person; they also learn what relationships are like. If care is mostly warm and dependable, they tend to expect support from others and feel more confident. If care is inconsistent, frightening, or neglectful, attachment can become less secure.

Containing damage from sudden disappearance of attached individual

When a child suddenly loses access to someone they’re securely attached to, it’s experienced a bit like a bereavement, and in some cases can be traumatic, but good support and substitute relationships can protect them a lot.

## **How kids build attachment:**

Kids establish attachment through repeated experiences of being cared for in a reliable, warm, and responsive way. When a caregiver notices their signals, comforts them, and helps them feel safe, the child learns, “This person helps me when I need it.”cpa+1

## **How it develops**

In the early months, babies mainly build attachment through everyday interactions like feeding, holding, eye contact, soothing, and consistent routines. Over time, these repeated responses create trust and a “secure base” from which the child can explore the world.ncbi.nlm.nih+1

## **What strengthens it**

* Responding quickly and sensitively to needs such as hunger, discomfort, fear, or tiredness.learning.nspcc.org+1  
* Being consistent and predictable, so the child knows what to expect.caring.childstory.nsw.gov+1  
* Offering comfort, affection, and positive attention through touch, smiles, talking, and play.eccpct+1  
* Letting the child explore while staying emotionally available as a safe base.greatergood.berkeley+1

## **What children learn**

Children don’t just attach to a person; they also learn what relationships are like. If care is mostly warm and dependable, they tend to expect support from others and feel more confident. If care is inconsistent, frightening, or neglectful, attachment can become less secure.cpa+1

If you want, I can also explain this by age: baby, toddler, or school-age child.

—

## **What can happen emotionally and behaviourally**

* Strong grief and protest: crying, clinging, anger, searching for the person, sleep and appetite changes.  
* Anxiety and separation worries: fear that other caregivers will also disappear, more difficulty with goodbyes, regression (toileting, speech, independence).  
* Changes in trust and behaviour: some children become withdrawn and “shut down”, others become more irritable, aggressive, or controlling if the loss/separation is prolonged or repeated.  
* If there are multiple separations or losses over time, risk increases for trauma symptoms, reactive attachment problems, and later emotional or relationship difficulties.

These outcomes are more likely and more severe when:

* The loss is sudden and unexplained.  
* There have been earlier disruptions, violence, or other traumas.  
* Remaining caregiving is inconsistent, frightening, or emotionally unavailable.

## **Protective factors and mitigation**

You cannot make the loss “not matter”, but you can massively reduce long‑term harm.

* Ensure at least one other stable, reliably responsive caregiver (often the other parent, grandparent, or very consistent adult) who becomes the child’s secure base: predictable routines, emotional availability, comfort on demand.  
* Keep the environment as stable as possible: same home where feasible, same school/nursery, same key adults and routines; minimise additional changes.  
* Name and validate feelings: explain in age‑appropriate, honest language what happened (“Mummy/Daddy can’t live with us now…”, “They died…”) and that the child is not to blame; expect repeated questions.  
* Maintain connections to the missing person when appropriate: photos, stories, rituals, memory boxes; this helps organise grief rather than suppress it.  
* Support other attachments: siblings, extended family, trusted teachers and caregivers can all offer extra emotional anchors if they are consistent and kind.  
* Watch for red‑flag signs (persistent nightmares, play dominated by loss themes, strong aggression, self‑blame, ongoing withdrawal or regression over months) and seek child‑focused, trauma‑informed therapy if they appear.

## **If separation is planned or partly controllable**

If you know a key attachment figure will become unavailable (e.g., long travel, illness, separation):

* Prepare the child with simple, concrete explanations, including who will care for them and what will stay the same.  
* Create predictable contact patterns if safe/possible (video calls, letters, set times), and stick to them to preserve some sense of reliability.  
* Gradually strengthen relationships with alternative caregivers beforehand (special one‑to‑one time, shared routines), so the child already experiences them as safe.
